newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Jochimsen - small group needed for timely EMU.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Jochimsen - small group needed for timely EMU.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said on Friday that Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU) could only start on time in January 1999 with a small group of qualified countries.

In the text of a speech delivered in Luxembourg but made available here in advance, Jochimsen also said that he did not support talk of delaying the EMU project but said the prospect of a delay should not be "categorically ruled out."
Maastricht criteria should not be softened, he said and all candidates to take part in monetary union should be judged on the same measure, not by a politically motivated "Gentlemen's Agreement."

"If the deadline set out in the treaty is to be kept, but if on the other hand there is to be no decision at the euro's expense, it follows that only a start with a small circle of really qualified countries can be considered," Jochimsen said.
That point made the EMU topic all the hotter, especially if "supposedly favourite" entrants are failing by large amounts to meet the convergence criteria for the euro, he added.
Jochimsen argued against any form of political motivation for the choice of EMU entrants, which he said "will not and cannot work."
"Anyone can bring up some kind of excuses and explanations. Therefore I say very clearly: All candidates must be judged by the same measure," he said.

Jochimsen said calls for immediate negotiations on a delayed start for the euro were wrong and said this risked disrupting the pressure on countries to pursue budgetary consolidation measures which were necessary whatever happened.
"On the other hand a delayed start should not be ruled out categorically in advance or even demonised as a 'question of war and peace'," Jochimsen said.
"It would be totally absurd to place a general ban on thinking and discussion as a form of political correctness."
Turning to Germany itself, Jochimsen said it would be "extremely difficult" for Germany to meet the budgetary criteria set down by Maastricht.
The Maastricht treaty calls on countries to keep their budget deficits at no more than three percent of gross domestic product.
